Ross Marquand reveals how the original X-Men animated series, metal singers, and even Jesse Ventura helped shape his voice for Apocalypse in X-Men '97.

In this Collider interview, Marquand breaks down the surprising process behind voicing both Apocalypse and Professor X. After receiving his Apocalypse audition while in New Zealand, he canceled plans to visit Lord of the Rings locations and spent two days studying clips of original voice actor John Colicos. Marquand explains how Colicos’ Shakespearean delivery became part of his foundation before he added a darker, bass-heavy quality of his own.

He also discusses why switching between Professor X and Apocalypse during recording proved difficult, eventually leading the team to record each character separately.

Beyond the booth, Marquand reflects on growing up as a Marvel and X-Men fan, being bullied for the things he loved, and the specific Wolverine moment that helped inspire him to become an actor. He also shares why he supports X-Men '97 pushing into darker territory, his emotional response to the season finale, and why he believes the original X-Men animated series helped pave the way for Marvel’s later mainstream success.

snippet.title: Fightland: A Tight Prison Cell Changed Duke’s Boxing | Collider Access
snippet.description:
Stunt coordinator Crispin Layfield reveals how Fightland built authentic boxing and deliberately messy street fights around Duke’s fighting style.

In this Fightland behind-the-scenes interview, Layfield explains why Duke’s opening boxing match was crucial to establishing his determination, discipline, and precision. Rather than making the heavyweight action overly flashy, the stunt team focused on movement that felt grounded and authentic, drawing comparisons to the way real heavyweights like Tyson Fury and Muhammad Ali move in the ring.

That boxing foundation carries into every fight Duke faces outside the ring. Layfield breaks down the challenge of staging a prison-cell fight with Duke handcuffed against two opponents, while still making his boxing background immediately recognizable. He also explains why street fights were designed to become scrappy and chaotic instead of looking perfectly choreographed.

The process required extensive rehearsal with stunt performers before teaching the actors each sequence section by section. Layfield also used previs, filming fights from multiple angles and editing them together before shooting, while remaining ready to adapt choreography to real locations.

For Layfield, believable Fightland fight choreography came down to precision, collaboration, and making a carefully rehearsed sequence feel anything but rehearsed.

Costume designer Kendra Terpenning explains how a Twin Peaks reference helped unlock one of Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’s most complicated costumes.

In this Collider interview, Terpenning goes behind the scenes of the 2026 movie’s costume design and reveals the surprising references behind Jane Schoenbrun’s slasher world. When developing the costume that emerges from the bottom of the lake, the team explored classic slasher villains, old-fashioned camping imagery, rust, water damage, vinyl, and latex. Then Schoenbrun proposed an unexpected reference: the plastic Laura Palmer is wrapped in when she is discovered in Twin Peaks.

Turning that idea into a functional costume required extensive experimentation. Terpenning explains how the team tested opacity, movement, sound, underwater performance, heat, restricted vision, and the physical demands placed on Jack Haven and their stunt double.

The interview also explores the subtler storytelling hidden throughout the movie’s wardrobe. Terpenning reveals how the “Flesh Palace” influenced Hannah Einbinder’s winter coat and the broader candy-colored palette, how costumes evolve alongside the characters, and why a pair of glasses became transformative for Einbinder’s performance.

She also discusses the movie’s more elaborate looks, from towering boots and a foot-tall mohawk to the unexpected amount of silk, velvet, and fur found in this unconventional slasher.
